# Design Levers {#sec-levers-ch}

A solar project is a long list of decisions, and almost all of them fall into six groups. How much ground to take. Which ground. What gets built on it. What grows there and how the place is run. Who holds the asset. What the parties signed. These are the **[design levers](terminology.qmd#term-design-levers)**, and they are the only things anyone can actually change.

Everything else in this document sits downstream of them. The [design pressures](design-pressures.qmd) are the forces arguing over how the levers get set, and the [restorative functions](restorative-functions.qmd) are what the settings produce. Two of those settings carry enough structure to need a chapter each: scale is read off the [scale transect](scale-transect.qmd), and the [sharing–sparing axis](sharing-sparing-axis.qmd) records what siting, structure, and management did to the farming between them.

| Lever | What it decides | What it can deliver |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Scale** | how much ground the project takes | the transect position, and how much of every other lever is left |
| **Siting** | which ground, and where on it | water quality, habitat context, service to nearby fields |
| **Structure** | what gets built, and how much earth is moved | microclimate, clearance for farming, light to the ground layer |
| **Management** | what grows, and how the place is run for thirty years | soil and carbon, habitat, most of the water balance |
| **Ownership** | who holds the asset and captures what it earns | a share of generation revenue for the people on the ground |
| **Contracts** | what the parties signed | the community function, durability for all of the above, and the alignment ownership stops supplying at scale |

: The six design levers. The first four act on ground and the last two act on paper, where ownership and contracts trade against each other along the transect. §-@sec-lv-menu lists the specific decisions inside each one, and §-@sec-lever-matrix reads the whole set against the transect. {#tbl-levers}

## Scale rations every other lever {#sec-lv-scale}

Every other lever is rationed by this one, which is why it comes first and why it earns a chapter of its own (§-@sec-transect). It is a decision for some parties and a constraint for others: a farmer with one parcel and a distribution line at the road has very little say in it, and a developer assembling acreage near a [substation](terminology.qmd#term-substation) has a great deal. Both are choosing, and only one of them knows it.

## The ground levers: siting, structure, and management {#sec-lv-ground}

**Siting** is the choice of ground, and it is the most powerful lever where a designer has it. It is also the first to disappear as scale grows. Placement decides whether a water-quality claim is even available, because the two routes want opposite ground: [avoided loading](terminology.qmd#term-fn-hydrologic) needs the impaired field itself, and interception needs ground between that field and the water [@schulte2017]. It decides whether a pollinator planting reaches anyone, since a forager works a radius of roughly 1.5 km and about 3,500 km² of US farmland sits inside that distance of existing and planned facilities [@walston2018]. And it is cheaper than the argument against it usually assumes: siting New York's entire 2050 build around biodiversity came to 0.17% above the least-cost case [@gallaher2026].

**Structure** is the hardware and its geometry. It is the lever that carries the [microclimate function](terminology.qmd#term-fn-microclimate) outright, because shade, the drop in vapor-pressure deficit, and the shelter of nighttime minima are products of geometry rather than of anything growing. It also decides how much earth gets moved, which is the least visible structural decision and one of the most consequential: a [racking](terminology.qmd#term-racking) choice made on cost sets the soil-carbon ledger for thirty years before any seed mix is chosen (§-@sec-fn-soil).

**Management** is what grows underneath and how the place is run across its life. It carries soil and carbon, most of habitat, and most of the water balance, and it is the only lever that can still be changed after construction. That cuts both ways: a planting that was right in year one can be undone in year four by a contractor doing exactly what the maintenance schedule says [@blaydes2022].

Scale rations these three against each other rather than uniformly. As a project grows, siting narrows and management widens, and they trade places at A3 (§-@sec-siting-latitude).

## The paper levers: ownership and contracts {#sec-lv-paper}

**Ownership** is who holds the asset, and it settles both who has standing to decide the rest and who captures what the array earns. An owner-operator, a cooperative, and a utility do not want the same things, and the differences show up in the [ground layer](terminology.qmd#term-ground-layer) rather than only in the accounts. [Barnyard shelter solar](archetypes.qmd#arch-barnyard) is the clean case at the small end: it is restorative because the person who owns the array is the person who owns the animals under it, and no agreement was needed to align them.

Ownership is also the lever the transect moves furthest, and it moves in one direction. At the farmstead the array belongs to the operator. Through the field and parcel zones it belongs to the landowner, or to a community-solar structure with many small holders. At landscape and regional scale it belongs to developer capital and then to a utility or an independent power producer, and the person on the ground holds a lease instead. The [lever matrix](design-pressures.qmd#sec-lever-matrix) (§-@sec-lever-matrix) records that shift as a row, and it is the row with the most riding on it.

The generation revenue moves with it, and that is the largest thing an [agrisolar](terminology.qmd#term-agrisolar) project creates. A lease pays for the use of ground and is not a share of what the array sells, so a landowner earning three to four times what the crop returned per acre [@sturchio2025croplands] is still being paid for land rather than for electricity. **Restorativity has an ownership question inside it, and the size of the lease payment does not answer it.**

That is what makes co-ownership, a community-solar subscription, and an equity stake in place of a rent restorative instruments rather than goodwill: each keeps some part of the generation revenue with the people who host the thing. Put the other way round, by A4 and A5 ownership is more often what restoration has to be defended against than what delivers it, which is why the [community and economic function](terminology.qmd#term-fn-community) is most at risk on absentee projects and most fully realized under local or shared ownership.

**Contracts** are what the parties actually signed. This lever carries the [community and economic function](restorative-functions.qmd#sec-fn-community) almost by itself, and it is also what makes the other five last: a seed mix is a management decision, and whether it survives to year twenty is a lease question (§-@sec-fn-community).

Contracts run against ownership along the transect, in a trade §-@sec-lv-mode sets out. The clearest published case for the paper side is this: solar lease income can make a conservation practice affordable that federal biofuel policy had made unaffordable [@sturchio2025croplands]. No ground was chosen and no hardware was changed. The restoration happened in a contract, which is the lever most often left on the table.

## Three things come out of a lever setting {#sec-lv-outputs}

The rest of this document is organized around them.

**A position on the transect.** Scale is read directly, which is why A0 through A5 are settings on one lever rather than an independent coordinate (§-@sec-transect).

**A position on the [sharing–sparing axis](terminology.qmd#term-sharing-sparing).** This one is jointly produced, and the [two-question reading rule](sharing-sparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions) in §-@sec-positions shows exactly how. Whether production continues inside the [footprint](terminology.qmd#term-footprint-influence) is settled by structure and management, since [clearance](terminology.qmd#term-clearance) and [row spacing](terminology.qmd#term-row-spacing) decide whether a tractor fits and the ground layer decides whether anything salable grows, and that question separates S1 and S2 from everything below it. What the ground was beforehand is settled by siting, and that question separates ordinary converted ground (S3) from idle ground (S4) and impaired ground (S5). So the sharing wing of the axis is built and managed, the sparing wing is sited, and reading a position tells you which levers were doing the work.

**The restorative functions.** Each of the six in §-@sec-functions comes from a particular lever or pair, which is what the middle column of @fig-functions-overview records. Ownership is the exception: it produces no function of its own, and instead decides who captures the ones the other levers produce.

## Restoration modes: choosing which lever does the work {#sec-lv-mode}

A project does not turn out restorative. Somebody decides which lever will carry that work, and commits the design to it. That choice is the project's [**restoration mode**](terminology.qmd#term-restoration-mode), and five of the six levers can be made to carry it.

- **[Siting-led](terminology.qmd#term-siting-led)** — put the array where the ground itself does the work. [Solar prairie strips](archetypes.qmd#arch-prairie-strips) are the case: the planting goes where the runoff already goes.
- **[Structure-led](terminology.qmd#term-structure-led)** — build the geometry to do it: clearance, row spacing, how much light the modules let through. [Barnyard shelter](archetypes.qmd#arch-barnyard) is the case.
- **[Management-led](terminology.qmd#term-management-led)** — take placement as given and put the ground cover, the grazing regime, and the operational calendar to work. Regenerative solar grazing is the case.
- **[Ownership-led](terminology.qmd#term-ownership-led)** — structure the holding so that no agreement is required, because the interests were never opposed. [Barnyard shelter](archetypes.qmd#arch-barnyard) is the case again, and for a second reason: the person who owns the array owns the animals standing under it.
- **[Contract-led](terminology.qmd#term-contract-led)** — write it into the lease, the ordinance, or the benefit agreement rather than into anything on the site. The [community and economic function](restorative-functions.qmd#sec-fn-community) runs on this one.

**Ownership-led and contract-led are the same problem at two scales.** An owner-operator needs nothing written down, because the party deciding and the party living with the decision are one person. A utility in another state needs everything written down, because they are not. So the alignment that ownership supplies for free at the farmstead has to be manufactured, clause by clause, as ownership moves up the transect: the lease term, the maintenance obligation, the benefit agreement, the decommissioning bond. **Contract-led restoration is what you need when ownership-led restoration is no longer available**, which is why contract-led restoration is nearly empty at the farmstead and the main instrument at utility scale, exactly where ownership has travelled furthest from the ground.

**Scale is not itself a restoration mode. It governs all the others.** Choosing to build five megawatts rather than eighty is not a way of doing restorative work; it is what decides which of the five stay open to the design. That is the argument the [scale transect](scale-transect.qmd) makes at length, and why that chapter can say which mode dominates at each zone (§-@sec-restoration-modes).

That may not hold. Solar's spillover benefits scale with perimeter and proximity rather than with area, which makes several mid-sized arrays a different ecological proposition from one large one at the same capacity (§-@sec-community-scale). If that argument survives measurement, choosing to build small and many *is* restorative work, and scale earns a mode after all. Nobody has run the comparison (§-@sec-open-issues).

Choosing the mode early is what keeps a design from spending itself on a lever that scale has already closed. At A4 there is little to be gained by arguing over ground the [interconnection](terminology.qmd#term-interconnection) queue has effectively chosen, and a great deal to be gained by writing the seed mix and the maintenance obligation into the lease. Naming the mode is how that gets decided on purpose rather than by default, and defaulting is how a project ends up with restorative intentions and gravel.

It also settles two things afterwards. What to copy: a design that worked because of where it sat will not transfer to a site without that ground, however carefully the rest is reproduced, which is the mechanism behind [design import](terminology.qmd#term-design-import) (§-@sec-rg-consequences). And what to check: a siting-led claim is verified against a map, a structure-led claim against a drawing, a management-led claim against a maintenance schedule somebody has to keep for thirty years, and a contract-led claim against a document that can be read.

## The levers couple, and they change at different speeds {#sec-lv-coupling}

The six are separable enough to name and not separable enough to decide one at a time. Row spacing and ground layer are a single decision rather than two, because crops differ in how much shade they will trade for relief [@weselek2019]. Edge treatment is simultaneously habitat design and [social-license](terminology.qmd#term-community-acceptance) design, and it costs land, shading, and room to farm. Grazing is a management decision that only works if the structure left clearance for the animals and the contract found somebody to keep them, which is why grazing arrangements fall apart for reasons that have nothing to do with grazing.

The couplings that matter most run from paper to ground, and the reason is that the levers get fixed at very different moments. Scale and siting are settled once and never revisited. Structure is fixed on the day the project is built. Ownership turns over in decades and contracts in years, while management is continuous and can be changed next season. Architecture has a name for this. @brand1994, after Frank Duffy, argues that a building is not one object but several layers of differing longevity, and that a design works when the fast layers can move without tearing the slow ones. @habraken2002 adds the part that matters most here: each layer has a decision-maker of its own.

Read that way, management is the fast layer and therefore the fragile one. It survives only as long as somebody is paying for it and somebody else is checking, and the levers that do the paying and the checking are contracts and ownership. This is not a new observation about designed landscapes. The Landscape Architecture Foundation reports that parts of many projects fail within a year or two of installation because maintenance staff had no voice during design and the designer's scope ended at the final walkthrough [@douglas2015]. A project can be sited perfectly, built correctly, and planted well, and still be gravel in fifteen years, because the levers that would have held it there were treated as paperwork rather than as design.

## The full menu of decisions {#sec-lv-menu}

The specific decisions inside each lever, for a reader weighing an actual proposal.

*Scale:* how much ground the project takes · the capacity it is filed at, and the [zone](scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones) that follows from it · interconnection posture, from [behind-the-meter](terminology.qmd#term-behind-the-meter) to transmission · whether to build once or to phase several arrays. Setting this lever rations every one below it, which is why it gets a chapter of its own (§-@sec-transect).

*Siting:* which ground the array takes · where on the parcel it sits · whether it stands upslope or downslope of the problem it might fix · how near it is to the fields it might serve · whether a landscape carries a few large arrays or many small ones.

*Structure:* mounting type (fixed, single-axis, dual-axis, vertical bifacial) · how high the panels sit · how far apart the rows are, and how much of the ground they cover · [pore-space](terminology.qmd#term-pore-space) configuration · [module technology](terminology.qmd#term-module-technology) (monofacial, bifacial, semitransparent, spectrally selective) · grading and site works · the built half of the edge (setback, berm, wall, fence line).

*Management:* what grows underneath, and how it is established · the mowing and grazing calendar · [stocking density](terminology.qmd#term-stocking-density) · how the array is operated ([tracking schedule, curtailment](terminology.qmd#term-tracking-curtailment)) · construction sequencing and traffic-lane discipline · the planted half of the edge (hedgerow, buffer, vegetative [screening](terminology.qmd#term-screening)).

*Ownership:* who holds the asset, and therefore who decides all of the above and captures what the array earns: owner-operator, landowner, developer, utility, cooperative, or shared · co-ownership or an equity stake in place of a rent.

*Contracts:* lease terms and duration · [offtake](terminology.qmd#term-offtake) structure · interconnection posture · [community-benefit](terminology.qmd#term-community-benefit) instruments (host or community-benefit agreement, PILOT and good-neighbor payments, community-solar subscription, decommissioning bond) · easements.

## Testing the six for gaps and overlaps {#sec-lv-completeness}

A set of six is only worth having if every decision a project makes lands in one of them. The test is to take the decisions this document names elsewhere, in the [full menu](#sec-lv-menu) above, in the [lever matrix](design-pressures.qmd#sec-lever-matrix) (§-@sec-lever-matrix), and in the design dependencies under each [restorative function](restorative-functions.qmd) (§-@sec-functions), and see where each one falls. Most land cleanly. The ones that did not are where the set earns its keep, because each forced a correction rather than a shrug.

[Screening](terminology.qmd#term-screening) lands in two levers at once, and that is the right answer rather than a defect. A berm, a wall, and a fence line are built and belong to structure; a hedgerow is planted, established, and kept, and belongs to management. Splitting them matters because the two halves fail differently. The berm is still there in year twenty whether or not anyone tended it, and the hedgerow is there only if somebody did. A project that promises visual mitigation and delivers it entirely in plantings has promised something with a maintenance bill attached, and the neighbor who objected is the person who finds out.

Two items in the older lever list turn out not to be levers at all. *Which ecological outcome is being aimed at* is an objective rather than a decision about the project, which makes it the [restorative goals](design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) pressure. *Which regulations and certifications apply* is not chosen by anybody building, which makes it [policy and permission](design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures). Both are real and both belong in §-@sec-pressures-ch, and a list that carries a goal and a constraint alongside actual choices is sorting three different kinds of thing under one heading.

Two definitions had to widen to hold everything. **Structure** covers grading and site works and not only hardware, because how much earth is moved decides both where the water goes and how much soil carbon is still there to build on, and no other lever owns it. **Management** covers the construction period and not only the operating life, because construction sequencing and traffic-lane discipline decide how much of the starting soil survives to be managed at all (§-@sec-fn-soil). Both widenings were forced by a decision that would otherwise have had nowhere to go, which is the useful kind of correction for a set like this to receive.

The set would be wrong in either of two ways. A decision landing in none of the six would mean the list is short; a decision landing in all six would mean the categories are not cutting anything. Scale was the near miss, and it is instructive: the case for leaving it out was that it governs the other levers, which is equally true of ownership. Treating the size of a project as a fact about a site rather than as a decision somebody made is exactly the move this chapter exists to prevent. A counterexample of either kind is among the more useful things this chapter could be sent (§-@sec-open-issues).
